title: Scaling Domestic Optics for Small UAS, C-UAS, and Precision Munitions
summary: Explore how domestic optics manufacturing supports small UAS, counter-UAS, and precision munitions through scalable production and reliable supply.
body_markdown:
Building more unmanned systems requires more than airframes, batteries, and flight controllers. For platforms that depend on visible or thermal imagery, production also depends on a reliable supply of optical assemblies.


The same requirement extends to counter-drone systems and optically guided precision munitions. Although their missions differ, these systems share a manufacturing challenge: delivering consistent optical performance in the quantities and on the schedules their programs require.


A lens that performs well in a prototype is an important achievement. Supplying that performance repeatedly, through a sustained production ramp, requires a broader set of capabilities.


For domestic optics suppliers, the challenge reaches from optical materials and precision fabrication to coatings, housings, assembly, and testing. For system manufacturers, understanding that chain is essential to building a credible production plan.


**Where Optics Fit**


Optics collect, transmit, filter, and focus light onto a detector. The detector converts incoming energy into an electronic signal, which processing hardware and software turn into imagery or other information.


Visible-light cameras generally capture reflected light. Thermal cameras detect emitted infrared energy, revealing temperature differences without relying on visible illumination. Their lenses require materials suited to the infrared wavelengths being used.


**Small UAS and unmanned systems**


On small unmanned aircraft systems, or sUAS, cameras provide imagery for reconnaissance, observation, inspection, and, in some configurations, navigation. Visible and thermal channels can supply complementary information.


The optical assembly must fit within the platform’s size and weight limits while delivering the required field of view and image quality. Those requirements influence the complete payload.


The Army’s


[research into compact, lightweight UAS optics](https://www.army.mil/article/290857/c5isr_center_research_enables_soldiers_to_see_farther_through_advanced_uas_optics) illustrates this balance: improving imaging capability while reducing the size, weight, and cost of the equipment carrying it.


**Counter-UAS systems**


Counter-UAS platforms often combine radar, radio-frequency sensing, and optical cameras. Each contributes different information. Visible and infrared imagery can help operators assess an object and maintain visual tracking after another sensor provides an initial alert.


Optics operate within a larger detection and response architecture. The Congressional Budget Office’s


[review of counter-drone technologies](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/62563) explains the importance of layered defenses and the limitations of individual sensing methods.


**Precision munitions**


Some precision munitions use optical seekers to collect information for guidance. Imaging infrared seekers form images that support target tracking; other weapons use different guidance approaches.


Javelin is a familiar example. Lockheed Martin’s


[public product overview](https://www.lockheedmartin.com/content/dam/lockheed-martin/mfc/pc/javelin/24-11303_TM_Javelin_Product_Card_R1_6.pdf) identifies a passive imaging infrared seeker as part of its guidance system.


These applications place different demands on optics. A compact airborne camera, a long-range surveillance system, and a seeker assembly cannot be treated as interchangeable products, even when they share manufacturing processes.


**The Production Challenge Extends Beyond the Lens Material**


Concerns about germanium availability have brought welcome attention to infrared optical supply. LightPath’s


[existing supply-chain guide](https://www.lightpath.com/blog/how-to-strengthen-your-infrared-optics-supply-chain-in-2026) explores that material and sourcing context.


But securing optical material addresses only one part of production readiness.


An optical assembly may also require precision shaping, specialized coatings, accurately machined housings, controlled alignment, environmental sealing, and performance verification. A constraint at any one of those stages can limit deliveries of the finished product.


Consider a manufacturer with sufficient material and lens-fabrication capacity, but limited coating throughput. Adding more fabrication equipment may increase the number of unfinished lenses waiting between operations without increasing shipments.


The same problem can arise in assembly or final inspection. Capacity must be evaluated across the manufacturing sequence, including the steps that are less visible than material production.


**Scaling Means Delivering Consistent Performance**


An optical design establishes the intended performance. A production process must deliver it consistently.


Small variations in surface shape, element position, coating performance, or mechanical fit can affect the finished assembly. As volumes grow, manufacturers need processes that control those variations and identify problems before substantial quantities are affected.


That requires appropriate tooling, documented procedures, measurement capability, and feedback between engineering and operations.


Yield matters as well. The number of parts entering a process is different from the number of assemblies that pass final acceptance. Scrap, rework, equipment downtime, and inspection capacity all influence actual output.


A useful capacity discussion therefore goes beyond how many machines a supplier owns. It asks how many conforming assemblies the process can deliver, how that output has been demonstrated, and what must change to support the next production level.


**Different Missions Need Different Manufacturing Paths**


Domestic optical capacity must accommodate a range of products.


Compact thermal payloads may favor small, lightweight assemblies designed for repeatable production. Longer-range surveillance systems can require larger optical elements, more complex mechanisms, and different fabrication and testing equipment.


Those differences affect tooling, process times, material utilization, and workforce requirements. They also affect how manufacturers allocate equipment across product families.


A production plan built around one compact lens cannot automatically be applied to a larger or more complex assembly. Likewise, experience producing sophisticated optics in small quantities does not by itself demonstrate readiness for a high-volume program.


The relevant question is whether a supplier’s manufacturing approach matches the product mix, delivery schedule, and performance requirements of the customer’s program.


**Domestic Supply Requires Visibility Into the Full Process**


Domestic manufacturing can improve engineering access, production visibility, and coordination when requirements change. Its value depends on understanding which activities actually occur domestically and where upstream dependencies remain.


Material origin, fabrication location, coating location, and final assembly are separate questions. Allied sourcing may also play an important role in a resilient supply strategy.


Recent


[Associated Press reporting on Ukraine’s drone-component dependencies](https://apnews.com/article/0715effbd80246ee535fd25220011f30) highlights thermal cameras as a difficult area to localize. It illustrates how domestic system assembly can coexist with dependence on imported components.


That distinction matters when assessing production resilience. Moving final assembly closer to the customer does not automatically create local capacity for every critical manufacturing step.


**Qualification Must Be Part of the Ramp**


Additional capacity becomes useful when its output meets the program’s requirements.


New equipment, tooling, materials, or process locations may require validation and, depending on the program, customer approval or additional qualification. Those activities belong in the production schedule.


Material alternatives are one example. LightPath’s


[work with the Defense Logistics Agency to qualify additional BlackDiamond™ glasses as germanium substitutes](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lightpath-technologies-awarded-phase-2-funding-in-us-defense-department-partnership-to-qualify-additional-germanium-substitutes-302262203.html) demonstrates the importance of establishing material readiness.


Application-specific evaluation still matters. Engineers must determine whether a selected material, optical design, coating, and assembly meet the intended operating requirements.


Planning that work early gives program teams more options and reduces the likelihood of discovering a qualification gap when deliveries are approaching.


**Better Demand Information Supports Better Capacity Decisions**


Manufacturers also need sufficiently defined demand to invest effectively.


An overall market forecast provides context, but a production plan requires more detail: which assemblies are needed, in what quantities, when deliveries begin, and how demand may change over time.


Clear product requirements help suppliers select equipment and tooling. Credible schedules help them plan staffing, qualification, and inventory. Forecasts should also distinguish development needs from funded production and longer-term opportunities.


Early collaboration allows customers and suppliers to compare those needs against realistic manufacturing lead times. It creates an opportunity to resolve constraints while the program still has flexibility.


**Build Optical Capacity Into the Program Plan**


For small UAS, counter-UAS, and optically guided munitions, production readiness includes the optical supply chain.


The strongest approach connects material availability with fabrication, coatings, assembly, testing, and qualified output. It also connects those capabilities with a clear understanding of customer demand.


At LightPath, our work across optical materials, components, assemblies, and thermal imaging supports that system-wide perspective. Early engagement helps customers evaluate performance requirements alongside manufacturing and supply considerations.


Scaling domestic optics means building the capability to deliver the right assemblies consistently—and having that capability ready when programs need it.
